correctness.rationale: The reduction from baseline is ηa(N−a)+η(b−ηa)(N−b), since the second filter treats an already diminished load. Substituting s=a+b and d=b−a gives constant minus ηQ/4 with the claimed diagonal coefficients and continuous center. The feasible s interval is centered at N, with integer half-length n−1−d. If parity disagrees this half-length is at least one because the maximum feasible d=n−1 matches N in parity. Thus all and only the nearest parity centers attain the fixed-gap minimum. Expanding adjacent scores gives 2[2(d+1)−η(N−d)] in matching parity and 2[2d−η(N−d−1)] otherwise. Their signs are those of τ_d−η, and alternating numerator and denominator changes make the τ_d strictly increase. With strict inequality in the gap count, equality adds precisely one adjacent gap; no increments at n=2 and thresholds above η=1 are handled by the same rule. The n=6 example gives three placements at each of η=2/3 and η=1. The reclassified continuous benchmark is valid: sources in an earlier gap are attenuated geometrically in later gaps, giving the stated quadratic form; the positive normalized inverse row sums uniquely solve it and are strictly feasible even at perfect removal. These statements assume postsite sampling and no decay outside the identical filters.

value.rationale: The two-filter model isolates the first interacting treatment choice: the first filter changes how much the second can remove. Exact thresholds and all ties distinguish weak and strong treatment on a fixed grid without exhaustive placements; at a crossing three different placements can be optimal despite uniqueness of the continuous relaxation. This is a sharp, reusable benchmark for discrete placement and an exact structural result rather than the covariance specialization alone. No field-performance claim is made.
